mainClaim: Universal healthcare systems deliver better health outcomes at lower costs than market-based systems
evidence: Himmelstein, Campbell and Woolhandler (Annals of Internal Medicine, 2020) compared 2017 health administration spending in the United States and Canada, which has a single-payer system. They found that US insurers and providers spent $812 billion on administration, $2497 per capita or 34.2% of national health expenditures, versus $551 per capita or 17.0% in Canada. The gap in administrative spending was large and widening.
supportingPoints: Preventive care access reduces expensive emergency treatments
Single-payer eliminates insurance profit margins and complexity
Negotiating power reduces drug prices 60-80% vs U.S. levels
Universal coverage improves productivity - workers less afraid to leave jobs

sourceMetadata.title: Health Care Administrative Costs in the United States and Canada, 2017
sourceMetadata.institution: City University of New York at Hunter College; Harvard Medical School; University of Ottawa
sourceMetadata.methodology: Analysis of government reports, provider accounting data, physician surveys and census employment data

limitations: The cited paper compares administrative costs in the US and Canada only. It does not cover other universal systems, life expectancy, infant mortality or medical bankruptcy. Transition costs and disruption significant. Wait times for non-urgent procedures can be longer. Taxation increases required. Cultural/political barriers in U.S. are substantial. Quality of implementation varies by country.
